text_fidelity_a:
SSK Aluminum M.2 NVME SATA SSD Enclosure Adapter, USB 3.2 Gen 2 (10 Gbps) to NVME PCI-E SATA M-Key/(B+M) Key Solid State Drive External Enclosure Support UASP Trim for NVME/SATA SSDs 2242/2260/2280 I tried to like this drive, i really did. The enclosure is nice, slim and compact. It assembles easy and feels like a solid build.

Sadly, I wouldn't buy this again due to the JMC583 chipset, it has nothing to do with the manufacturer SSK but rather the controller they use it the product...
I bought this after reading a ton of threads and reviews on the JMC583 chipset and how it worked pretty well with the latest firmware update. However, after getting this external drive kit and setting it up with a SamSung 970 EVO NVME drive and updating to the latest JMC firmware, it worked okay for Windows workloads but it had serious problems with Linux on a Raspberry Pi 4B. tons of UAS reset errors. Even tried it with the UAS bypass workaround and still it had resets.

Additionally, the drive gets really hot with use. hot to the touch and almost worrisome. I know this may be somewhat normal for NVME drive enclosures but it definitely feels above my personal safety threshold.

I'm going to try a different drive enclosure next with the RTL9210 chipset as I've read more favorable reviews on that.
text_fidelity_b: SSK Aluminum M.2 NVME SATA SSD Enclosure Adapter, USB 3.2 Gen 2 (10 Gbps) to NVME PCI-E SATA M-Key/(B+M) Key Solid State Drive External Enclosure Support UASP Trim for NVME/SATA SSDs 2242/2260/2280

text_fidelity_a:
MEE audio M6 X1 Wired In-Ear Sports Headphones with Microphone and Remote – Sweatproof Secure Fit Earphones for Running, Jogging, and Gym Workouts (Black) (EP-X1-GYBK) Even pre break-in, these sounded great: probably the best headphones under $20 I've found. After break-in, these MEE buds were sounding like something that cost 4-5 times as much with a nice, even frequency response that favors bass only slightly. I find them comparable to $60-$80 Sennheisers, my previous favorites (which superseded Sony and Koss buds that I also liked). These MEE buds came with 3 sets (S, M, and L) of your typical soft rubber earpieces as well as 2 sets of the interesting multi-tiered earpieces shown in the photos and a pretty standard cloth case. Between the various earpiece options, it's unlikely anyone will have an issue finding a good fit.

The cord is about 1 m long, which suits my purposes. I like the over-the-ear wire bits, too, as they prevent tugs on the cord from dislodging them. They might be awkward with some kinds of glasses, but my straight-earpiece sunglasses fit over them fine. They can be bent to hang down more like normal earbuds if desired, though.

I'll be checking out more MEE products now, seeing what a great value these were. I still favor AKG and Beyerdynamic at the high end, but for my biking/hiking/running/workout listening needs, I'll probably be coming back to MEE.
text_fidelity_b: MEE audio M6 X1 Wired In-Ear Sports Headphones with Microphone and Remote – Sweatproof Secure Fit Earphones for Running, Jogging, and Gym Workouts (Black) (EP-X1-GYBK)

text_fidelity_a:
Brainwavz S5 IEM Noise Isolating Earphones with Clearwavz Remote and Microphone for iPhone iPad iPod I’m a big fan of the Brainwavz S1 (actually all of their headphones – have yet to be disappointed with any of their products). The S1 has been my main set for active use (e.g., workouts, runs, etc.) since the flat cable is very durable and resistant to tangles. The S5 keeps all the good features of the S1 and adds to it – the sound quality is richer and better defined.

That’s not to say the S1 sounds poor – they are quite good, in fact. But the S5 are better. The highs are better defined and the midrange has more punch to it. The bass comes through clearly without moving into the harsh territory when the volume is pushed (as the S1s can do). The overall sound quality is very pleasing.

The build quality seems solid – as solid as the S1 or better. I love the flat cable! I know that’s something that is not appreciated by everyone, but for me it’s been working out wonderfully. Although this (as most other Brainwavz headsets) comes with an excellent hard shell case, I usually tote my earbuds wrapped around my mp3 player in my pocket. Easy to carry; very stressful on the cables and can lead to tangles with round wires. Flat wires, especially those with a thick jacket such as these, survive that abuse with zero problems.

The earbuds themselves are more sleekly shaped than the “can” style of the S1.

Comfort is in line with the customary Brainwavz style, which is to say it’s outstanding. It comes with a wide range of tips to fit pretty much any ear, plus the Comply foam tips (which are my favorite). If fitted properly you end up with zero ear irritation plus excellent sound isolation and bass response.

These are an over-the-ear design much like the S1. I never used that design prior to the S1 and it did take me a little time to get accustomed to it. It became second nature quickly, and the design is a lot more stable when exercising than the conventional in-ear design.

These are more expensive than the S1, but you can hear the difference in price. Still, if you’re looking to keep the cost down a bit, the S1 is an excellent performer as well.

Great sound, great comfort, wonderful cable design, and it comes with a solidly made case and lots of eartips. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Brainwavz S5 IEM Noise Isolating Earphones with Clearwavz Remote and Microphone for iPhone iPad iPod

I also found it to have more than good enough sound quality for watching movies, with the dialogue coming through clearly. It's not the best for listening to music (the mid and upper ranges are a bit constrained) but for it's intended purpose of a gaming set, no complaints at all regarding sound quality.

My major problem was with range. I love the fact that these are wireless, but placement is critical. I'd lose the signal if I didn't vary much from a specific spot near the wireless adapter. Moving just a bit out of the "zone" killed the connection. That was a disappointment since, while I didn't expect to be able to roam around the house with them on, I did expect to be able to leave my chair and go a short distance without breaking the connection. No problems with signal strength when seated or within a few feet of the adapter, but hit and miss when moving more than a few feet away.

Other than the range issue, this is a pretty good value in a gaming headphone set.
text_fidelity_b: Corsair Vengeance 2000 Wireless 7.1 Gaming Headset (CA-9011115-NA)

Sony BDP-S350 1080p Blu-Ray Disc Player I've had my Sony S350 Blu-Ray player for over a year now and here are my thoughts. The picture is completely amazing, even makes regular dvd's look better. I love that there's no more cords for picture and more cords for sound, just one HDMI cable and poof - high quality picture and surround sound.

A couple things to consider before buying your Blu-Ray player and subsequent Blu-Ray discs:
1. Blu-Ray will play your regular dvd's but if you have a regular dvd player (such as in your car) you cannot play Blu-Ray discs in it.

2. Patience is needed with this unit. After putting in a movie, especially if it is somewhat new, it could take 3-5 minutes to load. I am personally never in that much of a hurry to start the movie. While the movie is loading (a progress/status bar is provided on-screen) I can make popcorn, get the dogs situated, etc.

3. In conjunction with #2, the owner of this player must also be diligent about updating the firmware inside the player. I updated my player once last year (in November) and have noticed slower loads with current movies, so I plan to update it again next month (March). My guess is that it's good to update it 1-2 times per year.
What's involved in updating the firmware? I log onto a blu-ray firmware site, choose my model of player, then burn the update to a dvd disc. Place the disc in the player, it will read and update your firmware (took mine about 5-10 minutes as I remember). Afterward, your player will load movies more quickly.
Note: Loading never occurs during the movie, the only load-time that is experienced comes immediately after inserting the disc. Here's an example of the patience it takes to operate this blu-ray player:
Turn the player on - wait about 30 seconds for the unit to be able to receive or eject a disc (if you're trying to quickly eject a disc and run it back to the movie store, this can seem long!)
Insert disc and close - wait 3-5 minutes for movie menu to load

After that, you're set to go. For me, it's worth the wait and the trouble to keep it updated. I am quite sure that future models will require less patience and diligence, but for now this is the way it is. If you want extremely good quality with your movies, it's a wonderful addition to your home theater.
text_fidelity_b: Sony BDP-S350 1080p Blu-Ray Disc Player

I thought when I got this surge suppressor that the extension cord was meant to be used with it so you'd have a total of nine feet of cord if needed. Apparently, the extension cord doesn't actually fit the surge suppressor; the extension cord has three two-prong receptacles that you could plug, say, lamps and the like into, but you cannot plug the surge suppressor itself into it. The extension cord is clearly marked as being for two-wire polarized, as opposed to three-prong grounded, appliances. So that's more than a little misleading.

The surge suppressor looks heavy-duty, but you are cautioned in the packaging literature that it's not to be used with "sensitive equipment" like everything we use surge suppressors for: computers, TV, etc. You can't use it with things involving water, either, like aquariums. So what would I use it for? A blow dryer? I think not. To make it even worse, you are told to cover the receptacles on the extension cord if they are not in use. There are little plastic sliders that you're supposed to use for this purpose. But one of the sliders on the extension cord I received won't stay closed. China-cheap.

Belkin has some good products, but this one doesn't impress me very much. And the whole thing is packaged in one of those awful clamshells that you risk hurting yourself on when you take the scissors to it.

text_fidelity_a:
Altec Lansing iM227 Orbit MP3 Speaker Overall, I'm pleased with this speaker. It hits the mark where it counts the most -- great sound. It makes the audio output of the Kindle Fire sound SO much better!

I also like that it runs on removable batteries. Many of the other small speakers I looked at had an internal rechargeable battery. While that has some advantages, the fact that the Fire does not have a USB port means I'd have to charge them from an outlet (with an adapter) or on my PC. Plus, non-removable batteries can present a problem when they fail. The Altec Lansing uses 3 AAA batteries which are far easier to deal with. I still use rechargeables (either Eneloops or the Amazon Basic rechargeable) and get several hours of play time per charge.

The shortcomings relate to the cord. It's short (about 8 inches) and is very thin. It would be a much better product with a longer cord (about 12 inches) and a cord that's made of more substantial material. I can see the cord being a potential point of failure down the road due to its lightweight construction.

But overall, it's a good device and a great value (if you catch it on a price dip). Highly recommend as an add-on to the Fire.
text_fidelity_b: Altec Lansing iM227 Orbit MP3 Speaker

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st) I have an iPhone and PC for all my nerdy electronic gadget needs - why do I need anything else? I really didn't want an electronic device to read from - I'm old fashioned & like carting a paper book around, holding it in one hand folded back, flipping back and forth to re-read pages if I needed. I went kicking & screaming until I realized that I don't have anymore space in the house for my favorite books! So I caved and after some extensive research, I bought a Kindle Fire and a pretty pink leather case from Amazon.com - The options were good and the price was right - and it was in color! I received it in no time flat already programed & ready to start loading it up with books. I was pleasantly surprised with the feel, weight, size and convenience of reading that I explored it's other uses too. I like that fact that I can e-mail docs to my kindle like recipe .pdfs or play games the way I do on my iPhone - Go Angry Birds. I had to wait for HBO Go negotiations for Kindle to complete in June, but now that it's here, I love it - as long as I have internet connection!

Here is what I didn't like so much about it ... maybe something to review for upgrades - next generations...

It's too easy to accidentally press the power button on the bottom end and I can't count how many times I tried to shut down while I was in the middle of something. I lost all my bookmarks to A Song of Ice and Fire once - that was bad.
The power cable connection is very tiny - seems flimsy and also is next to the power button.
And while I have WiFi at home - sometimes I get a weak to no connection (at no fault to the Kindle), it's nice to plug in to the hub to watch movies or surf the Internets.
Oh and I still need to research this, but I like to know page numbers rather than a percentage (is there a setting?)

I can overlook all that - the good out weighs the negative
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire (Previous Generation - 1st)

text_fidelity_a:
Acer Chromebook, 11.6-Inch, CB3-111-C670 (Intel Celeron, 2GB, 16GB SSD, White) **Discontinued by Manufacturer** I'm typing this review on this Chromebook right now! I'm a graduate student, and I got tired of my Windows computer installing updates every time I opened my laptop. It was frustrating. I just wanted to open my laptop and get right to writing my homework. Now I can! It's also very lightweight, so I can easily bring it and all my books with me to class. It holds a charge for at least 2-3 days of active homework use and general internet fun for me. It starts up almost instantly when I open it! The screen size is fine, and I often have two windows open at the same time, side by side. I've been trying to read more articles online without printing them, and using online textbooks via my Kindle app. After a bit of a learning curve, this has worked out awesome, because if I have my Chromebook, I have ALL my textbooks with me, plus my course information, and my notebook to write things down. I love it. Plus, it doesn't get hot or make a whirring sound when you use it for a long time. I like that because I often use mine while I"m sitting on the couch.

Getting used to using the Chromebook had some hiccups. First, I recommend using Google Docs for writing because it has an offline mode. The Windows OneDrive and cloud version of Word works ok, but if your internet has any interruption, you can't keep typing. That's annoying. So use Google Docs, and don't worry about it! (But if you're working on a project with someone, and they use Word on a Windows laptop, you can collaborate with them no problem using the cloud version of Word.) Second, organizing my files confused me, until I realized that "Save As" is now "Move to folder.' Also, you can download a few files to your Chromebook, so if you need to upload an attachment to Blackboard, you can pretty easily. You'll use your Google Drive for much of your file storage. I did connect my OneDrive to my Chromebook, but it's through a third party app thing, and the connection always has to be redone, so I don't really rely on that, and I plan to move my OneDrive stuff to my Google drive soon.

The only thing that was really hard was setting up my Chromebook to print to my WiFi printer. Google cloud print is in beta, and in theory, it's awesome. When you're done setting it up, you could print to your home printer from anywhere, using your mobile device. However, Google your printer and how to set up cloud print, and give yourself some time to set it up. If you're in a rush, you should just plug your printer into your Chromebook.

Lastly, since many public schools are going Chromebook, I thought it was a good idea to get one myself. I'm working on getting my Master of Arts in Teaching to be an elementary/middle school teacher. Using one for my own schoolwork helps me be able to help students use their Chromebooks. Additionally, the price is so nice, I don't worry about having to ever replace my Chromebook, because if it was damaged by schoolchildren, I'd only be out about $160 (instead of $2000 for a Mac). I'm even thinking of getting one for my mom, since most of what she does online could be done on a Chromebook, too.

Oh, and one very last thing, the keyboard is really enjoyable to type on. The keys are spaced comfortably, and the individual keys make a nice clicky sound, are springy, and are nice and thin, for fast typing. I know that might sound weird, but I'm picky about my keyboards.
text_fidelity_b: Acer Chromebook, 11.6-Inch, CB3-111-C670 (Intel Celeron, 2GB, 16GB SSD, White) **Discontinued by Manufacturer**

That's because this one has a "pocket" for the device just like the soft ultrathins, which means you see the screen through a well placed cutout. It also has holes cut for the buttons, lenses, and ports. It is smaller from a length and width perspective than the ultrathin, but a bit deeper because the cover is thicker. It also has an elastic strap attached to the cover that can be turned around to hold the case shut. Only time will tell if that stays nice and tight or ends up sagging after use. Really, it doesn't need to be used often as the case will mostly stay shut by itself.

The one thing I don't like is the way you fold the front cover behind the back: it sort of seems too stiff, as if you're not really supposed to. It also folds at both joints, which keeps it from lying completely flat. The ultrathin folio has it beat in that case, although I like the Verve in better in most other ways.

text_fidelity_a:
VideoSecu 2 Heavy Duty PA DJ Club Adjustable Height Satellite Speaker Stand Mount - Extends 26.5" to 47" (i.e. Bose, Harmon Kardon, JBL, KEF, Klipsch, Sony, Yamaha, Pioneer and Others) 1B7 These are very flimsy stands. They may be ok with small speakers (e.g. small bookshelf speakers or monitors with 4" woofers) when set to the shortest possible height, but I wouldn't even think of putting a PA speaker on one of these. The dimensions of the base is 8" x 8". Unless you are planning to bolt them to the ground, you definitely don't want to put a speaker cabinet that is heavier than 10lbs or wider than 6" on one of these. Because of the single (and small diameter) pole design, stability is very poor, no matter what how much you tighten the screws or center-balance your speakers. The side arms that are supposed to cradle the bottoms of the speakers from the sides is a mechanically poor design. The platform that the speaker sits on is only 4" deep. Given that a lot of monitor speakers are deep and the weight is distributed in the front (woofer) and back (plate amplifier), front-back wobble will be nearly impossible to eliminate.

The only way to use these speaker stands in a safe way for 5.25" or 6.25" bookshelf speakers would be to bolt the bottom plates on a sturdy piece of wood or MDF that is at least 12"x12".
text_fidelity_b: VideoSecu 2 Heavy Duty PA DJ Club Adjustable Height Satellite Speaker Stand Mount - Extends 26.5" to 47" (i.e. Bose, Harmon Kardon, JBL, KEF, Klipsch, Sony, Yamaha, Pioneer and Others) 1B7

Three fan settings and yes two of them are not quiet. I leave mine on auto and unless I am working on a hot day, moving or writing tons of files, don't hear the fan at all).
The LED lights are not an issue for me, but I could see where in a dark room it would bother some folks. (electrical tape if it really errkks you).
Getting the settings the way you want them takes some trial and error, but once you have them you will most likely not mess with them again.
Drives are easy to add or remove, a couple screws, slide it in the slot.
I have found that if the drive has been formatted and contains data when you add it, you have to force mount it, but once that is done no issues.
So if possible initialize the drive in the enclosure.
This is ideal for novice of mid-level tech geeks, or folks who have a large media collection (Music, movies, photos, etc).
I have hooked it up directly to my Mac Pro and my Wireless router (Orbi) so anyone authorized to access the network can access the media files on it. So my Photos on one drive, Movies on two drives and music on the last drive.
I would highly recommend this to anyone wanting to create a media server.
It DOES NOT have RAID built-in, it can be added via software, but, for a few bucks more you can get the RAID version of this.

Mudder Portable USB Light Laptop Light for Keyboard Flexible Stick Dimmable Touch Switch LED White Light Lamp for Laptop Computer PC (Black) This is one of those simple but really useful gadgets to have. It's an LED light but, instead of a single bulb or two, it has a row of 10 bulbs arranged in a 6 inch span. The light output at it's brightest level is very bright - actually too bright in that you'll hurt your eyes if you look at the bulbs when they are at full brightness.

You turn the light on by tapping the end of the "bulb stick." Touch once to turn it on/off, press and hold while it is on to adjust the brightness. There's a wide range of brightness levels, from ultra bright to barely on. Unfortunately, it does not remember the last setting when you turn it off and then turn it on again. It always comes on at the brightest setting.

The stalk is very bendy but holds its position well. It's also very sturdy, with a metal rather than plastic casing. The total length is about 19 inches; the bendable stalk about 10.5 inches long. This is very thin - the bulb end is about the width of a pencil - so it's easy to fold up and stow in a tablet or laptop bag. Excellent build quality, especially considering the price.

It has a standard USB connector on the end for power. I've been powering it with a small powerbank and it draws very little power - leaving it on for several hours barely made a dent in the powerbank charge level.

I find this very helpful when using a tablet at night. I can bend the stalk so the light shines where I want it (the attached keyboard) but not on the screen. It's easy to stow when not in use - no wires or bits that get tangled up. Great value for the price.

CyberPower CP1350AVRLCD Intelligent LCD UPS System, DISCONTINUED * SEE NEW UPDATED MODEL CP1350AVRLCD3 * A UPS is one of those products you don't give much thought to until you are in a situation where you REALLY need it to work. The display on the Cyberpower is a great feature - tells you all sorts of useful info such as your battery status, run time, load level and others so you always know what's going on.

Nice footprint, puts out very little heat (compared to a Tripplite that this replaces which threw off a huge amount of heat - nice in the winter time, but not so nice in the summer), simple setup. My only complaint, and the reason it lost one star, is the spacing of the outlets. You have to use outlet extenders if you have the "wall wart" transformers. I have three of them (modem, router and external hard drive) - they all fit on the Tripplite since it offers widely spaced outlets, but couldn't fit them into the Cyberpower without extenders.

The other nit is the location of the power button. It's right on the face of the unit, and you have to be careful not to hit it accidentally. A better design would be to either locate it somewhere else or, better yet, put a safety lock on it so you can ensure you don't power down unless you truly want to do so.

Both are minor issues and can be easily worked around. I'm very pleased with the unit so far, and recommend it to anyone looking for a good UPS and a nice price.
text_fidelity_b: CyberPower CP1350AVRLCD Intelligent LCD UPS System, DISCONTINUED * SEE NEW UPDATED MODEL CP1350AVRLCD3 *

text_fidelity_a:
Kindle Fire HD 8.9", Dolby Audio, Dual-Band Wi-Fi, 32 GB (Previous Generation - 2nd) SEE BELOW FOR LATEST ON 5-3-13
SEE BELOW FOR LATEST ON 5-11-13 SECOND DEVICE GOING BACK TOO. SOUND FAILED.
SEE BELOW FOR FINAL REVIEW, ALL POSITIVE, 5-20-13

5-11-13 I REALLY DON'T KNOW HOW TO RATE THIS THING NOW. WHEN IT RUNS IT IS FINE. WHEN IT DOESN'T IT ISN'T. NOW THE SOUND HAS FAILED. CAN'T RUN PANDORA, ANY WEBSITE THAT PLAYS AN AUDIO TRACK WITH VIDEO OR MUSIC; CAN'T RUN MP3 OR MP4 FILES AND HEAR ANY SOUND. ANOTHER BEING SHIPPED TO ARRIVE HERE TUESDAY. I AM GETTING REALLY TIRED OF REBUILDING MY BOOKMARKS, APPS, PREFERENCES, ETC. I HAVE WASTED HOURS AND HOURS DOING THIS NOW. I WAS EVEN SO HAPPY THIS TIME THAT I BOUGHT MY WIFE A 7" FIRE HD FOR MOTHER'S DAY. I PRAY HER'S WORKS. I HAVE ALMOST COMPLETELY LOST MY FAITH IN FIRE HD.

The above, and the stuff I deleted from my first review had to do with screen flaws in the first and dead sound card in second. All cleared up and the cogent review comes next.

5-20-13

PROBLEMS RESOLVED WITH THIRD DEVICE. WHEN THEY WORK AND WITH SOME APPS TO SPEED THINGS UP, IT IS 5 STARS NOW.

While waiting for the 3rd device I checked around the web for quality issues with other vendors and discovered they all have problems now. The race to grab some market share is pushing new/re-designed devices out too fast and DOA and other issues are rampant in the industry. Amazom actually may be a bit better; the offset is that if you have a problem and get on the phone with them it is pretty easy to get a new device sent out for exchange via 2-day air, and you keep the one you have until the new arrives. That is an industry high mark that not all vendors have. So this took a lot of the sting out of flaws. Enough.

The device is beautiful, powerful and in 32 GB size has enough memory for most of us, even the video users or gamers who save lots of bytes.

I made the best change though by installing the Dolphin browser app and ES File Explorer. Doplpin is faster than Silk and more flexible. Also you can organzie folders for bookmarks very easily. ES File Exp is a tool you need. You can find almost everything on your device easily and manage apps and other files. They are both free and in Amazon store.

I use Last Pass and Xmarks to manage passwords and bookmarks on desktop/laptop machines and they both work very well with Dolphin. So I was able to load a lot of bookmarks easily that otherwise would have been typed in laboriously and taken hours.

I use Gmail because that gives me the perfect multi-platform email program.

I am a Latin student and found a couple of very good Latin apps. I also was able to find The Daily Missal Readings and an app with the Liturgy of the Hours, in both Latin and English. Both available in Amazon Store too.

When in range of Wifi I can do anything I need to do and do it well with the Kindle Fire HD 8.9" When operating stand-alone I have Latin-English books/Bibles on the device and the necessary dictionaries to continue translation. Very handy.

The only fault still, and I have complained about this repeatedly to Amazon, you can look up a foreign word from a book in German, Spanish, Portugese, French and Italian dictionaries, plus several Oriental tongues, but Latin is not a choice. You have to go to the web or type the word out into Google Translate, Whitaker's Words or some online program. It seems it would be easy to add the Latin dictionary as an option because several very good digital versions are around and I use two of them on an e-ink 1st generation Kindle device. Fix that Kindle and you get 10 stars!

In short, buy one but if you have trouble, get to them right away. Of course, read the instructions and make sure your complaint is not from lack of knowledge.

My final words on the subject.
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Fire HD 8.9", Dolby Audio, Dual-Band Wi-Fi, 32 GB (Previous Generation - 2nd)

StarTech.com 2.5in USB 3.0 SSD SATA Hard Drive Enclosure - Storage enclosure with power indicator - 2.5" - SATA 3Gb/s - 3 Gbit/s - USB 3.0 - black (SAT2510BU32) I'm using this enclosure for an earlier-gen SATA thin profile 500GB Western Digital hard drive and getting great results. The fastest removable media I own is a SanDisk Extreme USB 3.0 flash drive. And with this enclosure, the WD hard drive is hitting read/write speeds that are almost as fast as the SanDisk Extreme. It's not nearly SATA III fast (since it's not a SATA III drive), but fast.

I followed the recommendation of other reviewers and reformatted the hard drive to MBR and NTFS file system before using. This requires using DiskPart or Disk Management in Windows. Instructions are available on the web.

Older hard drives with a thick profile won't fit this enclosure. If you're not sure if your hard drive is thin profile and you don't have a metric ruler handy, if it's a quarter inch or less in thickness (and has a SATA connector) it's thin profile and will fit this enclosure.

I did not get good results testing the enclosure with a desktop computer with only USB 2.0 capability---it was very slow or not even recognized when plugged in. I don't want to blame the enclosure, because I've had similar issues with other brand enclosures and that same desktop computer. But I want to mention this in case you're thinking of buying this to use with a computer that only has USB 2.0. You might do better to get a USB 2.0 enclosure.
text_fidelity_b: StarTech.com 2.5in USB 3.0 SSD SATA Hard Drive Enclosure - Storage enclosure with power indicator - 2.5" - SATA 3Gb/s - 3 Gbit/s - USB 3.0 - black (SAT2510BU32)

text_fidelity_a:
Datacolor Spyder5EXPRESS – Designed for Hobbyist Photographers (S5X100) I ended up using this colorimeter to profile and calibrate my monitor. Out of the box I was not very happy with the quality of the product. You end up getting pretty much zero instruction and no manual. I had to figure it out on my own just by looking at the product. Once that annoyance was over I got to experience how terrible the default software from datacolor is.

I looked to the reviews and decided I could make the most of this purchase by using other free calibration software. I used Argyll and DispCalGUI. If you simply download DispCalGUI it will prompt you automatically to download the Argyll color libraries.

You then go into Tools->Instrument->install Argyll CMS instrument drivers...

This will download the drivers you need to run the spyder 5.

After this calibration is possible. I calibrated and it seemed to do a decent job. All in all, the calibration software looked like it was powerful--certainly better than the default.

In the end, I returned the product. I wanted something that would work without me having to go the extra mile to get it to work. At this point, with all of the extra I had to do to calibrate I still don't know if it did a good job or not.

Dimensions can be seen in the photos I have attached.

Included is the unit only.

Pros:
*Calibrates
*Decent price

Cons:
*Terrible OEM software (-2 stars)
*Setup--while not hard--is not immediately obvious. A small pamphlet would have gone a long way (-1/2 a star)

Additional Considerations:
Go for hardware that has good software calibration tools. You cant beat the two working in synergy.

Overall: 2.5/5 stars (>=.5 rounds up, <.5 rounds down) => 3 stars

If you have any further questions regarding the product in my review please leave a comment below and I will get back to you as soon as possible.
text_fidelity_b: Datacolor Spyder5EXPRESS – Designed for Hobbyist Photographers (S5X100)

text_fidelity_a:
Cisco-Linksys E4200 Dual-Band Wireless-N Router,Black I bought the Cisco E4200 and the Asus RT-N56U. The RT-N56U was better than the E4200 in strength and speed. Transferring files from laptop to NAS server was much faster with the ASUS both wired and wireless. I however decided to stay with the Cisco because the attached USB hard drive (NTFS) works flawlessly with Windows Backup (not the case with the RT-N56U).

Anyhow, I just switched to AT&T U-verse and tried to have the E4200 get an internet IP address automatically. For some reason it didn't. The ASUS here performed great, as soon as I plugged the cable from AT&T modem/router it configured itself. Amazing! Again... I need those backups in NTFS drives, otherwise I would stick with the RT-N56U.

After trying to troubleshoot myself and losing connection with their chat support, I had to call tech support (in India or surrounding areas). I spent almost hour and a half on the phone, resetting and rebooting everything. The router would just not get an internet IP address. They suggested that the router may be defective, but that I should call AT&T and see if there was something they could do on their end???

Instead of doing that, I drove to my sister house and got her E4200(I did the same setup in her house the week before and it worked well). When I plugged it in, it got the internet IP address immediately, no problems at all.

Both routers had the exact same firmware and settings which indicated to me that the problem was most likely with my E4200.

Again to call Cisco tech support. I explained what happened and told the tech that I had disconnected the router, and that I wanted a replacement. After many questions about how many PCs and laptops I had in my house -irrelevant to the case-, he asked me if there was a cable in lan port one, I replied NO, then he asked the same question about port 2, I replied NO, and so on, until he asked me if there was power going to the router, to which I obviously reply NO. So he said sarcastically 'how do you expect the router to work if it is disconnected?'. I replied 'what part of "I disconnected the router" you did not understand. Misunderstandings like this happened with all the technicians I spoke to.

Another one told me that I had voided my warranty for upgrading the firmware in the router. She scolded me for doing so stating that 3rd party firmware can have bricked the router. I explained to her that I downloaded the firmware from the Cisco support website. She kept going on. I am still trying to figure out where she got the idea that I got 3rd party firmware. What a show of ignorance!

When I asked for a supervisor, they put me on hold for 28 min. After that I was told that there was nobody available. Then the call got mysteriously disconnected when I asked the tech for his full name and badge number.

It is not only Cisco, I know. Many companies do it this way. But it is upsetting that Cisco can not source people who understand and speak English well enough to have a professional conversation. Based on this experience I wonder if these Cisco 'technicians' hold at least a high school diploma.
Yeah, they offer support 24-7-365, but it is not real support if they can not help you or even understand you.

My final advice, if you go for it, test the every single feature of the router. If you find any flaw, deal with Amazon, exchange it or get a refund. Do not try to deal with Cisco-Linksys. It is not worth the aggravation.
text_fidelity_b: Cisco-Linksys E4200 Dual-Band Wireless-N Router,Black

text_fidelity_a:
Inateck 3.5 Hard Drive Enclosure, Aluminum USB 3.0 Sata HDD Enclosure, FE3001 I've had this enclosure for almost 2 years. My five year old computer was very slow and I was having lots of trouble with it and the enclosure connecting to it. I did get it to connect and do one backup, but that was it. So, I thought surely it was my pc that was the problem. It would either not connect or it would not do anything...like I didn't have it plugged in. I just thought all three connections had to be made properly for it to come on and do it's job. I am not completely tech stupid, nor savvy.
I am disabled, so I was saving for a new computer. I have had lots of sickness over this time, and getting to this was not a huge priority and I never came back to read reviews. I wish I had.
I finally did recently get a new pc, and just the other day wanted to give it another go. When I plugged it in, again, there seemed to be no power... and then suddenly there was a burning smell and smoke coming from the enclosure where the power supply went in. It was quite scary, because I almost did not catch it soon enough.
I took a long shot and contacted the company anyways, even though it had been such a while to explain the long ordeal, and why I had not contacted sooner... Among my sickness, I was giving the device the benefit of the doubt, because I honestly thought it was my pc.
This is the message I received in return "In this case, it is highly commended to stop using this hard drive enclosure.
According to your information, this item is faulty. Regarding our products, a 12-month warranty is provided, however, it is obviously that the item ordered on 2016 has been far beyond its warranty. Hope that you could understand."
They did offer a 15% "return after purchase" discount refund if I would purchase a new one. But, as I am disabled, I cannot afford to do that at this time.
Hopefully, my backup really is on the hard drive that this unit supposedly saved it to that one time, as some beloved photos of my deceased father are on there, and I don't have them anywhere else.
I wish I were more tech savvy and didn't stay sick so much... Even so, I wouldn't have known the problem until I got a new pc anyways. Based on my experience and other reviews, I would not recommend this enclosure to anyone.
I do hope this helps someone.
text_fidelity_b: Inateck 3.5 Hard Drive Enclosure, Aluminum USB 3.0 Sata HDD Enclosure, FE3001

TP-Link AC1900 Smart WiFi Router (Archer A8) -High Speed MU-MIMO Wireless Router, Dual Band Router for Wireless Internet, Gigabit, Supports Guest WiFi I wrote this review with a heavy dose of input from my husband, who is a retired IT professional.

We had a problem with the router supplied by our internet provider. It was causing all the devices on the network to lose their connection multiple times per day. The provider sent us a new router, but it was a "black box" device that did not allow for configuration by the user or even the provider's tech support personnel. So we decided to buy our own router. After quite a bit of research, we picked this one.

PROS

-Good speed at 600Mbps for the 2.4GHz band and 1300Mbps for the 5GHz band.
-It is configurable by the user. I can sign on to the admin page via my browser and change settings. The setting we most wanted to change was the default DHCP server lease time setting. For a home network such as ours that always has the same devices using it, there is no need to have short (i.e., hours long) DHCP lease time setting. The constant renewing of the lease can cause connection issues for the devices. At least, that has been our experience.
-The device seems very stable. Since swapping it in for the internet provider's router, we have had no dropping connections whatsoever. We are quite pleased with this router.
-2 year warranty.

CONS

-The maximum DHCP lease time setting was only a couple of days, unlike a previous router I had, which allowed you to go up to 30. But this is not really a big disadvantage. I have not noticed a problem with it.
text_fidelity_b: TP-Link AC1900 Smart WiFi Router (Archer A8) -High Speed MU-MIMO Wireless Router, Dual Band Router for Wireless Internet, Gigabit, Supports Guest WiFi

Kindle Touch, Wi-Fi, 6" E Ink Display - includes Special Offers & Sponsored Screensavers I tried the first generation Kindle but didn't really care all that much for it. While I loved the screen, it just didn't feel right, and remember thinking this would be perfect if it had a touchscreen.

When the Touch was announced I ordered this along with a Fire with the thought that the Fire would be for me, and I'd give the Touch as a gift. The Touch got here this morning and I opened it up just to make sure it was OK. It looked so nice that I carefully peeled off the plastic just to try it out for a few minutes. After all, one wouldn't want to give a gift that didn't work, right? Well, it's now been a few hours and several chapters of a few books later. I'm keeping it. A second one will be on order for Christmas giving.

Why keep the Touch when I also have a Fire? If you skip over the obvious answer (I just love electronic gadgets) the e-ink on the Touch is much better in terms of clarity and lack of glare. Not that the Fire is bad. It has a very clear screen, but there is some glare. The Touch is better for reading under all lighting situations, and remains highly readable in direct sun. I can't imagine getting better screen clarity than this for black and white text.

I also tried reading it while on a treadmill (a situation that usually gives me a headache when I tried it using the kindle app on my Touchpad) and it was quite pleasant. Best of all is that I can zoom up the text size so I can read it while it is on the treadmill reading stand (it's too far away for me to read hard copy unless it's in HUGE type. Getting old is _not_ fun).

But the strength of the Touch is also it's biggest problem for me - black and white. I read several magazines each month and reading them in B/W is lackluster at best. Magazines are more enjoyable on the Fire, especially publications such as Wired.

The touch interface is great. So far its been very smooth and glitch free. Love the feel of the screen - has a bit of texture to it. I have to say, however, that I am a bit concerned about the screen longevity. The Touch overall feels a bit fragile and less "solid" than the Fire. I'm not deducting any stars for that since it's just an impression, but it will be interesting to see if the durability of the Touch screen is better/worse/same as the Fire (and vice versa). I'll be getting a case for it for sure since it's going to be getting bumped about.

I'll be using the Fire mainly at home and for reading material that works best in color (and, of course, video - need to relax the mind with mindless entertainment as well!). The Touch will be living in my briefcase for reading while commuting (I take the bus and subway, so lots of time to read) and for killing time prior to an appointment. The longer battery life and smaller size makes it a better traveling companion than the Fire. I don't have the Touch 3G version, so I'll have to make sure I keep a few books on my to-be-read stack so I don't run out when I'm out of wi-fi range.

Granted, if I could only have one device, I'd stay with the Fire since that offers more entertainment options, albeit at twice the price. But the cost is not excessive, so I treated myself to both. With a Fire and a Touch I've got all bases covered (until, of course, the next glittery gee-whiz piece of electronics comes out...).
text_fidelity_b: Kindle Touch, Wi-Fi, 6" E Ink Display - includes Special Offers & Sponsored Screensavers

It is strong steel, well finished and just right for rolling my 40" Vizio (which weighs only 17 lbs) around the patio for outdoor viewing at the optimal position and height. It looks great and functions flawlessly. It assembled easily. Though it comes with a sheetmetal wrench and a 4mm Allen, I used my own 8mm and 10mm sockets to speed assembly. And a 17mm end wrench to tighten the caster jam nuts. Sadly, one tiny nut was missing; I found a replacement from my personal metric collection of miscellaneous nuts and bolts. Pay close attention to the graphical instructions. I assembled the base upside down before realizing it was wrong. Easily remedied. Also comes with a collection of TV mounting screws, washers and spacers.

I was going to mount the TV on the wall, but being off to the side and quite high, that would very much limit viewing angles and no doubt strain necks. What I really wanted was to have the TV in front of me, wherever I might be sitting and also be able to optimize for group viewing if necessary.

This little cart is exactly what I wanted. It has 2" high quality urethane casters that roll effortlessly and silently on smooth surfaces. They aren't cheap hard plastic wheels. Each caster's threaded stem screws into a tapped hole. A jam nut on the threaded stem allows you to adjust the casters so all four are on the ground, then tighten the jam nuts to lock the adjustment. No wobble! You'll need a 17mm end wrench to tighten the nuts. Two of the casters are equipped with all-lock brakes that prevent both rolling and castering so the TV stays put if desired. When I'm done, I can simply roll the TV out of the way or into the house for safe storage.The base measures 18x20 inches. My 40" TV is 36" wide. You might think it would be top heavy or unstable, but it's not for me, especially as I have the mast set to near its lowest position.

The sturdy steel telescoping mast allows me to lower the TV so that the bottom edge of the 40" TV is 24" inches from the ground -- a few inches above coffee table height. This allows a very comfortable viewing angle when sitting in my somewhat lower patio chairs. In other words, it puts the TV at a very comfortable height to avoid neck strain.

The mount is adjustable and accommodates the 200x200mm Visa mount hole pattern on my TV. It can also handle 100x200 or smaller. Other stands have very large mounting bars. This one is small, simple and compact. Be aware its max Visa mount pattern is 200x200. You can adjust for level and tilt. It can tilt up about 15 degrees. It does not tilt down. The tilt is controlled by a knob. Be aware the TV is more or less permanently mounted onto the mast and the mast is bolted tightly to the base using five fasteners with locknuts: it does not come apart easily. If you want to disassemble this device for travel, you'll need to add thumbscrews.

I did not want extraneous things like extra shelves for a DVD player. It's clean and simple. Its price is very reasonable. With all the nuts and bolts tightened securely, there is no wobble anywhere.

Couldn't he happier. it's well engineered, strong, lightweight and portable.
text_fidelity_b: VIVO Mobile TV Cart for 13 to 50 inch Screens up to 44 lbs, LCD LED OLED 4K Smart Flat and Curved Monitor Panels, Rolling Stand, Locking Wheels, Max VESA 200x200, Black, STAND-TV07W

text_fidelity_a:
adidas RPT-01 Bluetooth Sport On-Ear Headphones - Night Grey, 2.8 x 5.6 x 7.5 Inches I wear headphones when I work outside, spring through fall. By the end of fall, that year’s pair is pretty nasty from hours of daily use and me sweating in them. Of course I clean them, but it’s impossible to *really* deep clean headphones.

So that’s what drew me to the adidas RPT-01 Sport Headphones: the description advertises “removable, washable knitted ear cushions.” Knit covers I can wash? Hooray!

But there’s no instructions in the box on how to remove the ear covers or the headband. It turns out the cushions aren’t as removable as advertised.The ear cups twist off the headphones (a gentle, counter-clockwise turn), but there’s still an inner plastic rim. I thought I’d be able to wash the knitted cover itself, but nope. And I nearly tore the cover trying to figure out how to remove it, until I found the manual online.

I can’t figure out how to get the headband all the way off. The black plastic lining is removable, allowing the headband to be pushed up. I worry the headband will tear quickly, as the holes that line up with the black plastic lining aren’t reinforced.

Sound quality is okay … as long as I don’t use the Control Knob.

The Control Knob is like a volume rocker and skip/go back button in one. But when I used it to change the volume and skip tracks, I had static that lasted for several seconds.

There is an adidas Headphones app, but I thought it was useless. The only advantage of the app is that it allows you to set up to 3 customizable actions for the other button on the headphones. Oddly enough, at the time of writing this review, the app was only available on Android. I wanted to test the headphones on an iPhone too, but could not because the adidas Headphones app wasn’t available in my country (USA).

Lastly, the headphones are so uncomfortable to wear that I can’t wear them for more than 10 minutes. If I were inclined to use them, which I’m not, mainly because of the static whenever I use the Control Knob. I have a small head, but these headphones are tight and squeeze my ears and head. The ear cushions are actually quite scratchy too.
text_fidelity_b: adidas RPT-01 Bluetooth Sport On-Ear Headphones - Night Grey, 2.8 x 5.6 x 7.5 Inches

text_fidelity_a:
Jaybird X4 Wireless Bluetooth Headphones for Sport Fitness and Running, Compatible with iOS and Android Smartphones: Sweatproof and Waterproof - Black Metallic/Flash These are very good Bluetooth earbuds for sports use. Construction is very lightweight, but still very durable. Earpieces are very secure when I'm running or working out at the gym and more than comfortable enough for hour-long workouts. Sound quality is pretty good out-of-the-box, but a little thin at the higher frequencies (especially noticeable with acoustic music). Fortunately, Jaybird has a great smartphone app you can use to equalize the sound. I was never very good at designing my own equalization profiles by ear, but the app has several ready made profiles so I just picked the one that sounded best with my favorite music (boosting higher frequencies more than lower frequencies). There is no noise cancellation, but noise isolation is very good with the included foam eartips (not the default eartips).

I really do not like that you need a special dongle to recharge this headset. You can't just plug a standard USB cable directly into these, like with most Bluetooth headset. This may have something to do with the headset's waterproof rating, but other headsets I own are also waterproof and can still be recharged with a standard cable. I am concerned that the proprietary charging dongle will get lost or broken or I will just forget to bring it with me when traveling.
text_fidelity_b: Jaybird X4 Wireless Bluetooth Headphones for Sport Fitness and Running, Compatible with iOS and Android Smartphones: Sweatproof and Waterproof - Black Metallic/Flash

SanDisk 128GB Ultra Fit USB 3.1 Flash Drive - SDCZ430-128G-G46, Black Because of scoliosis that makes sitting straight up in a chair painful, I do all of my small press work kicked back in a recliner with a wooden lap desk straddling the arms of the chair. I've got redundant cloud-based backups set up for my most important data, but I wanted to have a Time Machine backup as well. My Seagate 2TB portable was taking up valuable lap desk real estate (I have to have a graphics tablet handy for design work), so when it crapped out on me, I started looking for something else that might work better.

This little Ultra Fit is working just fine. I had to reformat it for my MacBook Pro, but after I did that, setting up Time Machine was easy. I excluded superfluous non-work items (movies, photos backing up to Google Drive, and my archival book files backing up to pCloud and the SDHC drive), so I can actually get a decent number of backups before Time Machine starts knocking off the older ones. And there's room for me to work on my graphics tablet.

Another reviewer said it's flimsy so best for leaving in place, which is exactly what I'm doing. I haven't had any problems with it so far, and it was a small price to pay for the extra insurance and peace of mind.

text_fidelity_a:
Ring Video Doorbell 3 – enhanced wifi, improved motion detection, easy installation Great wireless camera/doorbell. Hardware/software this is ideal. We live on a busy street so we were getting lots of notifications. The software allowed us to adjust where the camera sensed motion, cutting down "false" notifications. Easy to use.
Easy to setup and install. Took maybe 15 minutes from opening the box to having it up and running.
Convenient set-up and access via phone (iOS and Android) app. Added skill to Echo, so when someone sets of camera or pushes doorbell, we get a notification via Alexa, and an image on the Echo show. You can adjust how often and what notifications you receive in the app.
Night vision is pretty good as well. Another nice feature is you can access a "live" view anytime, notification or not.
Audio works well, so if you are in the basement, garage, at work, shopping you can talk to whomever is at your door.
If you carry your phone everywhere or have a smart home speaker (Google, Echo or maybe Apple?) you won't need the additional chime, phone and speakers have a decently loud sound.
I would suggest getting a second battery if you have a busy street or lots of activity. The app notifies you in plenty of time the battery is low and needs to be recharged (only takes a couple hours to fully charge). But a second battery extends the life and less work (but to be fair, one screw using included driver, slide off plate, slide battery out, set to charge and reverse process to put battery back in. With two batteries, the whole thing takes about two minutes. With one, you simply have a non-functioning doorbell/camera for a few hours. No biggie, just FYI.
Also there is an an App called Neighbors free to join and use. It lets you share "videos and notifications of criminal or suspicious activity. So if someone in your neighborhood is broken into or home is vandalized they can share the video and/or share a notice of the incident. Lost dog, share. Delivery thieves, share. So both kinda cool and scary.
Now the BAD. To access the video you have to pay a monthly fee ( now if you access the video within the first 30 seconds or so, you are golden, but if you have your hands full, or can't access your phone, you can't see the video, or back it up. While the basic few is like $40 ish a year. Higher for the next tier up. That is forever. And no easy way to back up to a local storage device. All files are on Rings servers.
Now if you know that up front, and $40 is no biggie. Then 5 stars.
But for me that is an issue.
text_fidelity_b: Ring Video Doorbell 3 – enhanced wifi, improved motion detection, easy installation

ULANZI T2 Adjustable Tablet Holder for Desk, Carbon Steel Tablet Stand for Bed, Flexible Tablet Arm Clamp Compatible with iPad Pro, iPad Air, iPad Mini, Galaxy Tab, iPhone & 4.6-12.9 Inch Devices I wanted to use the ULANZI T2 Adjustable Tablet Holder to suspend my iPad Air 4 over my bed. I’ve already tried using a gooseneck holder to hold my iPad, but it was wobbly and every time I moved, the iPad bounced. So I thought the spring-loaded design of this one would prevent wobbling.

There are no assembly instructions inside the box. It’s not rocket science, but I shouldn’t have to look at the product page to figure out how to put it together. Instructions would also be helpful to show all the adjustability options for the various angles.

The mounting clamp only has a usable opening of 1¾ inches, so I’d advise double checking the width of where you want to mount it. I have a desk beside my bed that I used to mount the tablet holder, and I lucked out that the front of the desk didn’t have a metal frame underneath it. Otherwise, it wouldn’t have fit.

The tablet holder part held my iPad Air, with my iPad in a thin TPU case. The sides of the tablet holder have silicone pads (the clamp does too) to prevent scratching the tablet. But the grips aren’t too deep, so they won’t accommodate a thick case or device.

Unfortunately, this metal tablet holder had the same problem as the gooseneck one: it’s wobbly. It starts out okay, but I have to keep tightening the various screws, or my iPad wobbles. I also feel like it’s unsteady when stretched to the maximum length, so that impacts how I have to position the tablet holder.
text_fidelity_b: ULANZI T2 Adjustable Tablet Holder for Desk, Carbon Steel Tablet Stand for Bed, Flexible Tablet Arm Clamp Compatible with iPad Pro, iPad Air, iPad Mini, Galaxy Tab, iPhone & 4.6-12.9 Inch Devices

While I can't attest to the longevity of this reader as of yet, so far it's been a great performer.

It is USB 3.0 compatible, and worked fine on a USB 3.0 port on a Win 7 machine. It also worked just as well (albeit slower) on a USB 2.0 port on a Win 7 and an XP machine. Simple plug and play, with no drivers needed. It comes with a USB cable.

There are 5 card slots. I only used the CF and SD slots since those are the cards that I use. No problems with card insertion or removal. There's a visual indicator of read/write activity.

In addition to moving items to your hard drive, you can also do card-to-card data transfers.

The reader is compact, measuring just under 3.5 inches long and about 1.75 inches wide. It's very low profile, standing about ½ inch tall. The card slots are on the front, and the USB connection is on the back.

Simple, straightforward and works well. That's pretty much all I need in a card reader. Hopefully it will last longer than my previous one - I'll update the review should this not perform well over time.

Philips BT2500B/37 Wireless Portable Speaker I have owned those annoying bluetooth ear pieces that always feel like they're about to fall off - or actually do. And although the sound varies from product to product, it's just not a system I am comfortable with.

This little speaker is simply perfect for my needs. It is 4 inches by 4 inches wide and only 1 inch thick. It has a switch that you slide to the right when you wish to enable the bluetooth, or to the left to turn it off. There is also another small button right beside the switch that you push in to receive or disconnect a call. A silver volume knob is sleekly incorporated in the overal design. The pairing was instant and consistant. No need to type in some code or wait forever for them to find each other. But here's the most important part - I hear my calls clearly and with no drop off or fade.

In all fairness, I only use this in my car and I don't spend ridiculous amounts of time on my phone when I'm driving. I've used other products with useless results. Half of the time I would risk a ticket by just ditching the ear piece and talking on my cell. In this case, I'm able to place it on the seat next to me and converse without any problems. Now that it's passed my tests, I'll be getting some velcro and mounting it to my dash board when I'm driving, and then just popping it in the glove compartment when I'm done.

The unit comes with a USB charger cable and it had a partial charge when I received it. Once it's fully charged and you turn it on, a blue light will blink for about 2 seconds and then go to a solid blue. According to the enclosed instructions, you will know that the battery is low when it blinks red. Couldn't be easier.

Musically speaking, my JBL and Sony are better designed for that purpose. But as a compact, speaker phone - this Phillips is without equal. Hands-free clarity without an annoying piece of plastic hanging over your ear. What more could you ask?
text_fidelity_b: Philips BT2500B/37 Wireless Portable Speaker

I don't do Podcasts or self-centric Youtube videos. But, I DO videos about drones and quadcopters. Some of which, I narrate. I've always wanted to have a better audio experience for my viewers. Now, I have it. This Eivotor professional microphone is exactly what it says in the name, PROFESSIONAL. The quality of the sound recorded (to my ears) couldn't be better if it was done in an actual studio. Part by part... The mic itself is so well made, I couldn't think of a single criticism. It's just, simply stated, a professional quality mic. The stand is super sturdy, solid and easy. The cage is the perfect example of how to isolate 'telegraphed' noise from your desk or table, preventing unwanted noise in your recording. The mic has an open cell foam wind screen, like any pro mic would have. The 'pop' screen is great for those of us that over enunciate our consonants. I don't do that! (roll eyes) The connections are standard, the three prong mic connection can be swapped out for any length you happen to have around. The other end is a standard 3.5mm 4 c jack (designed for splitting the signal between your recording device and headphones). But, it can be used without the splitter pigtail, in case you don't need the feedback. You can tell from my brief video, the recorded sound is very good. Great purchase, five stars.

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Technology Speaker - for Portable use - USB This speaker set sounds great for its size. The sound is loud and clear, but also full in the way you would expect stereo sound to be. It is also small enough to travel fairly easily, although it is not the smallest on the market. This is capable of getting louder than you'll ever be able to use in a hotel room, but suitable for an apartment; there are plenty of options out there in the form of travel speakers.

The built in mic is obviously a significant factor, and it works great compared to my laptop mic. I do like the fact that it gets its power and signal over one cable, but sometimes I think I'm going to run out of USB ports since I use them regularly to charge my phones and other devices. And I was also expecting bluetooth after seeing the ads for the other models. But who cares about bluetooth when you still need power?-smaller speakers don't need an external power source.

This is a good product and I'm certain to use it, especially when travelling for long enough that I want to set up more of a "home" that includes music. It is sort of another take on what is already a niche product, however, and although I do think it's one of the better styles on the market, it's still not the end all of small speakers, nor does it make dramatic improvements over what is already available. It's great at packing full sound into something very portable, and it eliminates one cable if you use USB, but then you use up another USB port. I'd love to see it either fully wireless with included battery or also include a webcam to preclude the need for other accessories. Yes, I know these things would up the cost, but it would make a truly remarkable product.

I also like how the invisible button panel appears when powered on, but not how you can't completely turn it off without removing the power source. The speaker looks good and I like how all sides are covered in speaker screen material, but I worry I could easily stick my finger through a cone.

A quality product that is great if it closely fits your needs.
text_fidelity_b: Creative Technology Speaker - for Portable use - USB

I could click on a movie title and see what services it was one (and which ones I had free access to and which ones I would have to pay for it on). WAVLINK USB 3.0 Universal Docking Station with DVI/HDMI Dual Monitor Docking Station,2 USB 2.0 Port,2 USB 3.0 Port,Gigabit Ethernet,Quick Charging,Supports for Windows Mac OS The links on their site for the software download were not working, so I ended up having to go directly to DisplayPort to download the update. After that it was pretty smooth sailing.

I have kiddo all hooked up with dual monitors and his laptop docked and stored. So, now he has actual room at his desk to put his notebook or textbook or whatever else he needs for school, without the laptop taking up half his space.

To avoid any latency issues you can sometimes get while gaming and using DisplayPort software, I did hook his main monitor up directly to his laptop and "mirrored" the screen. This is the one he will play his games on. For his second monitor used for videos, research, etc. I used the HDMI port on the Wavlink dock and "extended" the screen. This way he can have dual monitors and bypass any latency issues that sometimes can crop up. If you can, it is also recommend when gaming to plug the mouse directly into the laptop as well, rather than the dock.

Personally, I don't notice any latency issues on either monitor or when the mouse is hooked up through the dock. But it was easy enough to just bypass the issue all together by how I plugged stuff in. The only struggles I had were with setting up his laptop to not go into hibernate instead of sleep after 2 hours, to stop disabling power to USBs while in sleep, and to allow his keyboard to wake the system out of sleep even though it was clearly already set up to do so. But that is nothing to do with the dock, and everything to do with Windows 10 being a pain in the behind sometimes. Finally everything is all set up, behaving as it should and we are ready for school to start next week. Well I'm ready, him... not so much.
text_fidelity_b: WAVLINK USB 3.0 Universal Docking Station with DVI/HDMI Dual Monitor Docking Station,2 USB 2.0 Port,2 USB 3.0 Port,Gigabit Ethernet,Quick Charging,Supports for Windows Mac OS

Jawbone Big JAMBOX Wireless Bluetooth Speaker - Graphite Hex - Retail Packaging The first thing I noticed when I opened the box was how small the Big Jambox is. It's truly portable and the name is more accurate of its sound quality. The first thing I noticed when I turned on the unit was that it talked to me and charted out the steps to pair the speaker to the iPhone 5. The second thing I noticed was the sound. The big full sound. I have truly eclectic tastes. My music collection includes rock, blues, jazz, world music from Africa, the Middle East, and the Lapland of Norway. I listen to didgeridoos from Australia, fiddles, marimbas, and jaw harps from Kyrzykstan. The quality is so good Im a bit blown away by the technology. The clarity is a wonder when listening to vocal qualities of choir ensembles, Bobbie McFerrin, , solo clarinets, and horn sections as well as my favorite twangy African and Middle Eastern instruments. The bass is great considering the speakers size. I predict I will enjoy my symphonic classical music more from now on.
But be reasonable, put it in perspective. Don't expect your Big Jambox to take the place of the power of a live stadium U2 concert or the knock-you -on-your-ass sound wall that passes through your body from a live large brass section of a jazz band orchestra, or be loud enough to overwhelm 10 or 20 loud drunk party goers. Don't be a bonehead! It flabberghasts me that anyone would criticize this speaker. If you actually listen to the sound quality of singers and instruments, or enjoy deep full sounds, spend the money (im on the cheap side) and get the Big Jambox. And dats da facts Jack.

Dell WM123 Wireless Optical Mouse (PXK14) This is your average, no frills cordless mouse. It is nearly identical to the Amazon Basics cordless mouse: http://www.amazon.com/gp/product/B005EJH6Z4/ref=oh_aui_detailpage_o04_s00?ie=UTF8&psc=1

As of the writing of this review the Dell mouse costs 17.82 + 3.17 shipping for a total of $20.99. That's not much money to spend on a cordless mouse but the Amazon Basics only costs $11.49 with no shipping. And it works a bit better in my humble opinion. The Dell turn wheel rotates a bit rougher than the Basics model, but does have slight finger indentations but I cannot notice if it's more comfortable than the Basics. It started instantly (as did the Amazon Basics mouse) with nothing done other than put the battery in the mouse, insert the antennae in the USB port and turn the mouse on.

The only thing that I really didn't like too much was the shrink wrap plastic nuclear proof packaging. It was quite a struggle to finally free the mouse and it's antennae. Basics are much easier to open and I don't recall any plastic packaging.
text_fidelity_b: Dell WM123 Wireless Optical Mouse (PXK14)

Lexar LNS200-960RBNA NS200 2.5” SATA III (6GB/S) Solid-State Drive 960GB I used this as cache acceleration in my Network Attached Storage (NAS). Used this way, it is like getting 240GB of almost-RAM for less than the price of 8-16GB of real RAM. This is a very general comparison, but the speeds of a good SSD like this are comparable.

If you want to upgrade your laptop from HDD to SDD, you can use Macrium Reflect software, which is free, and I have used for a few laptop upgrades in the past. 240GB is plenty for a Windows O/S and programs and some slosh space. Perfectly acceptable if you have a place for longer term storage.
